language: en
example_product: a fictional booking app for small pilates studios
page_type: SaaS landing
audience: Owners and front-desk staff of small studios who take bookings through chat apps and spreadsheets.
awareness: comparing_solutions
tone: businesslike, warm, unpretentious; formality 2; second person, plain
promise: {product} gives {audience} {main_benefit} without {pain}.
logic: The result and the first step come first, then proof that similar studios already use it. Pains and features come in matching pairs, and the steps sit before the prices, so the price is read by people already convinced that starting is easy.
threads:
- The promise of no more phone calls returns in the hero, in the steps and in the closing call.
- The hero and closing buttons use the same words, and a risk line sits under every button.

## p01 hero | Hero | b01
role: Say within five seconds what changes for the reader, and offer the first step.
- eyebrow "Eyebrow" | 3-5 | the main change for the reader | No more booking calls
- h1 "Headline" | 7-11 | the result for {audience}, without the product's name | Clients reserve a reformer, and you stay with the class
- subheadline "Subheadline" | 13-19 | how {product} delivers {main_benefit}: three parts separated by commas | Timetable, payments and reminders behind a single link that lives in your studio's bio.
- button "Button" | 2-4 | verb + object, the action {cta_action} | Set up bookings
- risk_line "Line under the button" | 5-8 | {risk_remover} | Free to start, cancel at any time
techniques:
- Keep {product}'s name out of the headline; it first appears in the subheadline.
- Build the headline from two short statements joined by a comma: what the reader does and what the product does.
- List three parts in the subheadline, separated by commas, and explain none of them.
tone: businesslike, warm; formality 2; you
avoid: "innovative"; a question as the headline; exclamation marks

## p02 social_proof_logos | Who already uses it | b02
role: Show that studios like the reader's are already here, before any explanation.
- line "Line" | 7-12 | how many and who: {customer_count} | Over two hundred pilates rooms now take every reservation this way
- 6 x logos "Logo":
  - name "Customer name" | 1-2 | {customer_n} | Core
techniques:
- State the number and the kind of customers in one line, with no praise.
- Show customers the reader's size, not the biggest names.
tone: restrained; formality 2; impersonal
avoid: "leading companies"

## p03 problem | The problem | b03
role: Let the reader recognise their own working day of manual bookings.
- h2 "Headline" | 5-8 | {pain} in the reader's words | A booking system made of chat threads
- 3 x pains "Pain":
  - h3 "Title" | 2-4 | a scene from the working day ({pain_n}) | Calls mid-session
  - p "Description" | 15-21 | what happens and how it ends | The phone rings during a reformer session while the room waits for you to settle somebody's slot for Thursday.
techniques:
- Describe every pain as a concrete scene from the working day, not as an abstract problem.
- Do not mention the product in this block.
- End the last pain with lost clients, money or time.
tone: sympathetic, concrete; formality 2; you
avoid: the word "problem" in the headline

## p04 features | Features | b04
role: Show that the product removes each pain from the previous block.
- h2 "Headline" | 5-8 | what leaves the reader's hands | The admin that used to be manual
- 3 x cards "Card":
  - h3 "Title" | 2-3 | a noun ({feature_n}) | Self-service reservations
  - p "Description" | 15-22 | what changes for the reader | Clients see which machines are free and reserve one themselves, even while you coach with the phone face down.
techniques:
- Each card answers one pain from the previous block, in the same order.
- Name each card with a noun; let the description say what changes for the reader.
tone: businesslike, confident; formality 2; you
avoid: a list of technical functions

## p05 how_it_works | How it works | b05
role: Convince the reader that starting is easy, before the price comes up.
- h2 "Headline" | 5-8 | the path from start to the first result | Live bookings in one evening
- 3 x steps "Step":
  - h3 "Title" | 2-4 | an imperative verb ({step_n}) | Enter your sessions
  - p "Description" | 14-20 | what the reader has after this step | Pick times, machines and instructors once, and the coming weeks fill in from that single setup.
- link "Link" | 3-5 | see {product} without signing up | Browse a sample timetable
techniques:
- Start every step with an imperative verb.
- In each description, write the reader's result, not an action in the interface.
- End the last step with the reader back at their own work, not at the product.
tone: simple, confident; formality 2; you
avoid: technical terms; more than three steps

## p06 testimonials | Testimonials | b06
role: Let the reader hear people in the same situation as theirs.
- h2 "Headline" | 3-6 | a plain title, no wordplay | Heard from studio owners
- 3 x quotes "Quote":
  - quote "Quote" | 18-30 | {testimonial_n}: the change, before and after | My evenings went on replying to reservation texts. These days I glance at the timetable over coffee and already know who is coming in.
  - who "Who" | 3-8 | name, role and kind of studio | Name, owner of a three-machine studio
techniques:
- Each quote names one concrete change: how it was and how it is.
- Take quotes from different roles: an owner, a front-desk person, an instructor.
tone: lively, conversational; formality 1; first person
avoid: quotes without a name; general praise

## p07 pricing | Pricing | b07
role: Help the reader choose a plan and see that the price matches the studio's size.
- h2 "Headline" | 4-8 | the price tied to the reader's size | Pay for the size you are
- toggle "Toggle" | 2-3 | monthly or yearly | Monthly · Annually
- 3 x plans "Plan":
  - h3 "Name" | 1-3 | the studio's size | Single room
  - price "Price" | 1-3 | {plan_n} | [price] / mo
  - for_whom "Who it is for" | 8-14 | who picks this plan | For a one-room studio with a handful of instructors
  - features 3 "Bullets" | 2-6 | what is included, most important first | Self-service reservations / Client reminders / Card checkout
  - button "Button" | 2-4 | its own action for each plan | Start here
- risk_line "Line under the prices" | 6-10 | {risk_remover} | Free to start, cancel the plan at any time
techniques:
- Name the plans after the studio's size, not after levels such as basic or pro.
- Open every plan with who it is for, and only then say what is included.
- Put one line under the prices that removes the risk.
tone: transparent, calm; formality 2; impersonal
avoid: asterisks and fine print

## p08 faq | FAQ | b08
role: Remove the last objections before the closing button: moving data, payments, cancellations.
- h2 "Headline" | 2-4 | a plain section name | Your questions
- 4 x pairs "Pair":
  - question "Question" | 5-10 | {objection_n} in the reader's words | Can I import my existing timetable?
  - answer "Answer" | 22-34 | yes, no or an action, then what to do next | Yes. Upload your current file and the sessions, instructors and machines show up in the timetable. Look them over once before the link goes public.
techniques:
- Open the answer with a plain yes or no, or with the action the reader takes.
- Use the second sentence for what to do next or what happens after.
- Phrase questions the way the reader asks them, not the way the product names things.
tone: calm, concrete; formality 2; you
avoid: "of course"; links to terms instead of an answer

## p09 cta | Closing call | b09
role: Repeat the main promise and offer the last, simplest step.
- h2 "Headline" | 7-12 | the hero's promise in other words | Leave the next reservation to the client, not to you
- line "Line" | 12-18 | when the reader sees the result | Build the timetable this evening, and by tomorrow clients are reserving machines with no help from you.
- button "Button" | 2-4 | the same words as in the hero | Set up bookings
- risk_line "Line under the button" | 5-8 | {risk_remover} | Free to start, cancel at any time
techniques:
- Repeat the hero's promise in other words: the reader already knows the product.
- Make the button repeat the hero button word for word.
- Put the same risk line under it as at the top.
tone: confident, no pressure; formality 2; you
avoid: urgency without a reason
